edge: concurrency fundamentals: floor = shared address space, race via load/add/store interleave, false sharing = perf not correctness, Amdahl 1/s, default-shared scoping of outer vars; ceiling = none found here (solid)

OpenMP construct semantics: floor = parallel runs block once per thread, unordered; ceiling = does not know static vs dynamic schedule, reduction identity init, which constructs have implicit barriers (master), believes tasks spawn a new thread each (thread pool/team model missing)

prep.capability: Read a C program, decide whether and how to parallelize it with OpenMP (independence, scoping, synchronization, reduction, scheduling, tasks), write the pragmas, and explain the benefits and the limitations (speedup bound, overheads, false sharing, bandwidth, memory model) at exam level.

environment.compiler: gcc 13.3 -fopenmp (_OPENMP 201511; 5.x constructs such as masked and atomic memory-order clauses are accepted)
environment.spec: OpenMP 5.2 for wording; gcc behaviour noted separately

exit_criteria.text: Given a C loop nest, decide whether it can be parallelized as written, what dependence blocks it, and what construct or rewrite (reduction, scoping, ordering, restructuring) makes it parallel; write the pragma with clauses.

variants.question: Decide for each loop whether it can be parallelized as written; if not, say what blocks it and give a race-free OpenMP version with clauses.
variants.answer: Loop 1: as written, s and m are shared accumulators updated by every iteration: a data race. Fix: #pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:s) reduction(max:m). Loop 2: a true loop-carried dependence (c[i] needs c[i-1] from the previous iteration): not parallelizable by a pragma; it is a prefix sum, which needs an algorithm change (two-pass scan) to parallelize. Loop 3: hist[k] with k data-dependent: two iterations may hit the same bin: a race. Fix: #pragma omp atomic on hist[k] += 1, or reduction(+:hist[0:bins]).
required: loop 1: shared accumulators race; reduction(+:s) reduction(max:m)
loop 2: c[i-1] is a loop-carried dependence; not parallelizable as written; needs an algorithm change (scan)
loop 3: same bin from different iterations races; atomic on the update or an array-section reduction
disqualifying: says loop 2 can be fixed with a clause
treats the max as safe because it only reads a[i]

hints: For each loop, name the memory locations written and ask whether two different iterations can touch one of them.
A dependence on the previous iteration's result cannot be removed by a clause.
Worked: loop 1's s is written every iteration: same location, no ordering: race; the reduction gives each thread its own s and combines them.

exit_criteria.text: Explain a synchronization choice: which construct makes an update race-free, why, and what it costs; recognize when atomic is insufficient and when a barrier is required or must be avoided.

variants.question: Every thread computes a partial result and then must (1) add it to a shared total, (2) append a record to a shared log with a shared write index, and (3) after everyone is done, thread 0 prints the total. For each of the three steps say which OpenMP construct you use and why the alternatives are wrong or wasteful.
variants.answer: (1) atomic update on the total: a single memory update, indivisible, cheaper than critical. (2) critical (or a lock): the index increment and the write to log[index] are two coupled operations on two locations; atomic covers only one update. (3) A barrier so all additions are done (the region-end barrier if the print is after the region, or #pragma omp barrier before a masked/single block inside it); masked alone has no barrier.
required: atomic for the single shared update
barrier before the print because masked has no implied barrier / region end has one
disqualifying: says atomic protects both the index and the log write

hints: Count how many memory locations each step updates.
Which constructs end with an implicit barrier?
Worked: step 2 touches idx and log[idx]; between the read of idx and the write to log another thread can run; only mutual exclusion around both is correct.

exit_criteria.text: Explain benefits and limitations: the speedup bound for a given serial fraction, fork/join and synchronization overhead, false sharing and memory bandwidth as reasons a correct program does not scale.

variants.question: A correct parallel loop over 10^8 doubles (c[i] = a[i] + b[i]) gets 1.6x on 8 threads; a loop that does 200 flops per element on the same arrays gets 7x. A colleague says the first loop must still have a bug. Explain what limits each loop and what Amdahl's law does and does not say about this.
variants.answer: Neither is buggy. The first loop does one add per 24 bytes moved: it is memory-bandwidth bound, so extra threads share the same bandwidth and stop helping once it is saturated. The second is compute bound, so it scales close to the thread count. Amdahl's bound (1/(s + (1-s)/p)) is about the serial fraction of the work; it does not model bandwidth, overhead or false sharing, which can cap speedup even when s is nearly 0.
required: first loop is memory-bandwidth bound (few flops per byte)
second loop is compute bound so it scales
Amdahl bounds the serial fraction only; bandwidth/overhead are separate limits

hints: How many bytes move per floating-point operation in each loop?
What resource is shared by all 8 threads regardless of the code?
Worked: 24 bytes per add; 8 threads ask the same memory system; once it is saturated, time is set by bytes/bandwidth, not by threads.

exit_criteria.text: Tasks: explain when tasks fit better than loops (irregular or recursive work), that tasks run on the existing team, what taskwait/taskgroup order, and the default data scoping of task variables.

variants.question: You parallelize a recursive tree walk with tasks. Say (1) why a parallel for does not fit, (2) how many threads run the tasks and where the tasks wait to be run, (3) what taskwait guarantees and does not guarantee, and (4) what the default data-sharing of a variable declared outside the task but inside the parallel region is, and why that default exists.
variants.answer: (1) The work is a recursion of unknown shape, not a countable iteration space. (2) Only the team's threads; tasks are queued and picked up by whichever team thread is free. (3) taskwait waits for the child tasks of the current task, not for grandchildren (use taskgroup for the whole subtree). (4) firstprivate by default for such variables, because a task may run after the creating scope has moved on, so it needs its own copy of the value at creation.
required: tasks fit irregular/recursive work that is not a countable loop
tasks run on the existing team threads, queued
taskwait waits for direct children only; taskgroup for descendants
outside-declared variables are firstprivate by default in a task, because the task may outlive the scope

hints: What does a for loop need that a recursion does not have?
Where did the threads come from?
Worked: the creating thread continues; if the task read the original variable later the value might be gone; firstprivate snapshots it.

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 §1.4.1 Structure of the OpenMP Memory Model
sources.note: 'Any other access by one task to the private variables of another task results in unspecified behavior.' 'If a data race occurs then the result of the program is unspecified.'

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 §5.1.1 Variables Referenced in a Construct
sources.note: 'Variables with automatic storage duration that are declared in a scope inside the construct are private.' Loop iteration variable of a loop-associated construct is private. In a parallel construct without default clause, other variables are shared.

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 §5.3 List Item Privatization
sources.note: New list item 'has an undefined initial value'; original's value after the region unspecified when aliased/accessed in the region.

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 §5.4.4 firstprivate
sources.note: 'For variables of non-array type, the initialization occurs by copy assignment.'

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 §5.4.5 lastprivate
sources.note: value from 'the sequentially last iteration of the associated loops' is assigned to the original.

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 §5.5.2 OpenMP Reduction Expressions
sources.note: 'The number of times that the combiner expression is executed and the order of these executions for any reduction clause are unspecified.'

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 §5.5.4 Table 5.1 implicitly declared C reduction identifiers
sources.note: + 0; - 0 (deprecated); * 1; & ~0; | 0; ^ 0; && 1; || 0; max = minimal representable; min = maximal representable.

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 §5.5.5 reduction clause semantics
sources.note: copies 'initialized with the initializer value of the reduction identifier'; 'the original list item is updated by combining its original value with the final value of each of the private copies'. Array sections since 4.5.

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 §15.2 critical construct
sources.note: unnamed critical: 'as if an identical (unspecified) name was specified'; executed 'as if only a single thread at a time among all threads in the contention group'.

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 Nesting of Regions
sources.note: 'A critical region may not be nested (closely or otherwise) inside a critical region with the same name. This restriction is not sufficient to prevent deadlock.'

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 single construct
sources.note: 'executed by only one of the threads in the team (not necessarily the primary thread)'; 'An implicit barrier occurs at the end of a single region if the nowait clause is not specified.'

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 masked construct
sources.note: 'No implied barrier occurs either on entry to or exit from the masked construct.'

sources.title: OpenMP 5.2 Deprecated Features
sources.note: master construct deprecated (since 5.1) in favour of masked.

sources.title: OpenMP 5.1 §2.19.7 atomic construct
sources.note: forms read/write/update/capture; update shapes x++, x--, ++x, --x, x binop= expr, x = x binop expr, x = expr binop x; without memory-order clause 'the effective memory ordering is relaxed'; 'A strong flush on the location designated by x is performed on entry to and exit from the atomic operation'.

sources.title: OpenMP 5.0 §2.17.2 barrier construct (wording unchanged in 5.2 §15.3)
sources.note: 'Each barrier region must be encountered by all threads in a team or by none at all'; 'The sequence of worksharing regions and barrier regions encountered must be the same for every thread in a team.'

sources.title: OpenMP 5.0 §2.9.2 worksharing-loop schedule kinds (unchanged in 5.2 §11.5.3)
sources.note: static: chunks 'assigned to the threads in the team in a round-robin fashion in the order of the thread number'; no chunk: 'approximately equal in size', at most one chunk per thread. dynamic: 'Each thread executes a chunk of iterations, then requests another chunk'; default chunk 1. guided: chunk proportional to unassigned iterations / threads, decreasing to chunk_size (default 1). auto: compiler/runtime. runtime: OMP_SCHEDULE. No clause: def-sched-var (implementation defined). Static reproducibility: same assignment in two loops with equal iteration count, same chunk (or both absent), same parallel region.

sources.title: GCC libgomp: OMP_SCHEDULE and FOR construct implementation
sources.note: gcc's no-clause default is static (compiler generated); schedule(runtime) with OMP_SCHEDULE unset falls back to dynamic,1. Two different defaults.

sources.title: GCC libgomp OpenMP 5.1 feature status
sources.note: masked and scope supported since GCC 12; gcc 13 accepts #pragma omp masked in C although _OPENMP reports 201511.

sources.title: C11 §5.1.2.4 Multi-threaded executions and data races (N1570)
sources.note: 'Any such data race results in undefined behavior.' Applies to a C program compiled with gcc -fopenmp alongside OpenMP's 'unspecified'.

corrections.what: n4 label and card cuo6fg: 'parallelizable iff independent' now scoped to 'as written'

corrections.what: n3 label: constructs also order work

corrections.what: n1 label, cards c3eld3/c3kqx8: stack location replaced by the spec's data-sharing rule
corrections.why: OpenMP 5.2 §5.1.1: variables declared in a scope inside the construct are private; 'one per thread's stack' is how gcc implements it, not the rule.
